title: Why Can Towering Mountains Stand on Pluto at −240°C?
description:
Why Pluto's Frozen Heart Has Zero Craters

Why can towering mountains stand beside a flowing glacier between −226 and −240 degrees Celsius (−375 to −400 degrees Fahrenheit)? On Earth, water ice is a soft glacier that melts, and rock is the solid ground beneath it. At Pluto's extreme cryogenic temperatures, water is rock-like — and Pluto's two to three-kilometre (6,500 to 9,800-foot) mountains are big blocks of water ice, sometimes coated with frozen gases like methane, standing beside the flowing nitrogen glacier of Sputnik Planitia.

Sources: NASA Science, Pluto Facts — −226 to −240 °C (−375 to −400 °F) surface temperatures where water is rock-like, 2 to 3 km (6,500 to 9,800 ft) water-ice mountains sometimes coated with frozen gases like methane, and crater-free convecting nitrogen plains (https://science.nasa.gov/dwarf-planets/pluto/facts/) · NASA Science, New Horizons Mission — 14 July 2015 Pluto flyby and ~1,000 km (600-mile) Sputnik Planitia nitrogen glacier (https://science.nasa.gov/mission/new-horizons/).

Pictures: NASA/JHUAPL/SwRI New Horizons LORRI and Ralph/MVIC imagery (PIA20732, PIA20473, PIA20726, PIA20198, PIA19842, PIA19952, PIA19936, and 14 July 2015 flyby sequence) and NASA Blue Marble Earth (PIA18033) alongside original animated explainers, with AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute (New Horizons, PIA20732, PIA20473, PIA20726, PIA20198, PIA19842, PIA19952, PIA19936); NASA Goddard Space Flight Center/Reto Stöckli (Blue Marble Earth, PIA18033).
